paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas Brayton was an armed attack by a mob on the house of a Black man at or near Paoli, Orange County, Indiana, on the night of Sunday, July 31, 1881. The defenders drove the attackers off with gunfire, and the mob withdrew carrying its wounded, with no one in the house reported hurt. An Indianapolis paper praised the armed defense as an example, while a wire brief carried the story to papers in the Dakotas and Minnesota.
According to the wire account, a mob sent word to Brayton, described as "colored," that he would be hanged. Neither report gives any reason for the threat or any accusation against him.

The Indianapolis Leader reported that "a gang of fourteen Orange County roughs on horseback and wearing masks" set out on Sunday night to mob a Black man living near Paoli. Warned in advance, he gathered three armed friends at his house, and when the gang ordered him out he answered with a shot. The attackers fired revolvers into the house, the men inside replied with shotguns, and after the second round one attacker was found badly wounded and the gang retreated with him.

The wire version differs in its details. In it Brayton barricaded his log house with two women inside, who loaded his guns while he kept up a fire on a mob "fifty strong." The mob answered "in a straggling way" and then dispersed, "carrying away five or six wounded comrades."

No report of arrests, an inquiry or charges against the attackers was found, and neither account names any of them. The Indianapolis paper said it had not learned the defenders' names but predicted they would "hereafter" be respected in their community.

The first report found ran in the Indianapolis Leader on August 6 under the headline "Bully for Paoli," with the subhead "A Case That Doesn't Need the Attention of the Governor." It mocked the attackers as "brave knights of the golden circle" who fired "in regular ku-klux style," called the wounded man a "villain," and said the defenders had set a good example for "their more timid brethren."

By contrast, the wire brief that named Brayton ran without comment among crime items. It appeared on August 12 in the Bismarck Tribune, the Grant County Herald and the Jamestown Alert, and on August 20 in the Warren Sheaf's "Weekly Record of Crimes."

The two accounts disagree on the size of the mob, fourteen masked horsemen in the Indianapolis report against fifty in the wire brief. They also differ on the defenders, three armed men in one and two women loading for Brayton in the other, and on the attackers' wounded, one against five or six. Only the wire names Brayton, so the match between the two accounts rests on place, timing and outcome.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Brayton
bases: A mob sent word that it would hang a Black man and then besieged and fired on his house, but was driven off by gunfire from inside (A1, A2).
Nobody was reported killed: the mob of fourteen (A1) or fifty (A2) was repelled, so this was an attempted lynching, not a completed one; no reason for the mob's threat was printed (A1, A2).

An Indianapolis report (A1) and a separate wire brief (A2) agree that a mob came at night or by notice to a Black man's house near Paoli, was met with gunfire and withdrew carrying wounded, though they differ on numbers and on who was in the house, and only the wire names Brayton.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Leader report
accounts.gist: Fourteen masked, mounted Orange County roughs set out to mob a Negro near Paoli on Sunday night; warned, he gathered three armed friends, and after two rounds of fire one attacker was badly wounded and the gang fled.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: A mob sent word to Thomas Brayton that he would be hanged; he barricaded his log house with two women who loaded for him, and the mob of fifty, returning fire 'in a straggling way', left carrying five or six wounded.

framing.detail: Headlined 'Bully for Paoli. A Case That Doesn't Need the Attention of the Governor,' it called the attackers 'roughs' and 'brave knights of the golden circle' and said the defenders deserved 'much credit' as an example to 'their more timid brethren.'
Western papers ran the same short brief, without comment, among crime items such as a 'Weekly Record of Crimes'.

conflicts.note: The Indianapolis report is closer to the scene (same state) and more detailed; the wire figure may be inflated, but neither is clearly better.
